raw_response:
I've been farming this land for 30 years. My father farmed it before me. I know what this soil wants, I know Quzhou's water situation, and I know what my neighbors are doing. Some of my family works in the city now, so I'm managing more of this alone than I used to be. That changes a few things — I don't want to waste time or water.

**My thinking on wheat:**
I plant wheat every October on all my land, then follow with maize. That's how it's always been done here and it works. I'll use the improved seed I bought from the county extension station — Jimai variety. I'm not going back to the old seed, the yield difference is real. For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea at jointing. I use 3 irrigations — one at sowing to get good germination, one at jointing, one at heading. The groundwater here is getting harder to pull up, so I don't water more than I have to. Two pesticide sprays: one herbicide in early spring, one fungicide when powdery mildew shows up. I'll rotary till before sowing to work in the maize stubble.

**My thinking on maize:**
Right after wheat harvest in June, I plant maize directly without tilling. No time and the moisture is better preserved. Hybrid seed — Xianyu 335, same as last year, good yield. Maize gets more nitrogen than wheat because it's a heavy eater. Rainfall June through August usually covers some irrigation, but I'll pump twice if it's dry at tasseling or grain fill. Two pesticide passes — herbicide early, and I watch for corn borer.

decision.reasoning_summary: All 30.4 mu rotates between winter wheat and summer maize on the same land each year. For wheat I use improved seed from the county station, apply compound fertilizer plus urea top-dressing at jointing, irrigate three times with the well to protect groundwater, and rotary till after maize harvest to manage stubble. For maize I switch to hybrid seed and no-till direct seeding right after wheat harvest to save time and soil moisture — some family labor has moved off-farm so efficiency matters. Maize gets heavier nitrogen and only two irrigations since summer rain usually helps. Pesticide use is minimal and targeted: herbicide plus one disease or pest spray per crop.
